doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Integrated Minton's group and bebop's social agenda
summary: Katz felt no problem in the integrated group and explains bebop as a music white players could not copy easily and a break from vaudeville.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was it out of the ordinary for this — this was an integrated group at the time — was it out of the ordinary?

Yes, but not as much as it is now in a way. I mean curiously now — this should be another discussion. I didn’t feel any problem. I have felt the problem at various times but not this time. I don’t know why. It would be interesting to go into that. But later, you know bebop had a social agenda as you probably know, when I say bebop I mean that’s not a secret — I don’t know if they did it consciously or not — but when Kenny Clarke and Monk and Dizzy and all those people made that music at Minton’s, part of the rationale was to come up with something that the white guys couldn’t copy so easy. And beyond that the idea that the time for jazz to be Vaudevillians had to stop. Because the fact of the matter is, and a lot of critics know this, I think the younger critics might have a better handle on it, but some of the older critics had this kind of — I’m not going to name names — the earliest critics, this is just my opinion, I’m editorializing now, this is strictly my opinion, and still prevails in certain quarters, where they look at black jazz musicians as some kind of noble savages.
